content: 1. Plasma transfusion is being investigated as a potential intervention to prevent intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) in very preterm infants. This protocol is part of a Cochrane Review aimed at evaluating the efficacy and safety of this intervention. 2. The primary objective is to determine whether administering plasma transfusion within the first 24 hours of life can prevent IVH in preterm infants born at or before 34 weeks of gestation. Additionally, the review seeks to assess whether plasma transfusion is associated with any adverse effects. 3. Advances in neonatal care have significantly improved the survival rates of preterm infants with birth weights under 1500 grams. However, the incidence of long-term neurodevelopmental disabilities remains high in this population. 4. The risk of neurodisability is particularly elevated in the smallest and most critically ill preterm infants. However, it is challenging to predict which infants will develop severe neurological, motor, or cognitive impairments. 5. Germinal matrix intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) is a common complication in preterm infants, occurring in approximately 20-25% of those weighing less than 1500 grams. Most cases are diagnosed within the first 48 hours after birth. 6. The presence of IVH, especially severe forms, is strongly associated with an increased risk of adverse neurological outcomes. Severe IVH is classified as Grade III or IV according to Papile's classification system and is linked to poor outcomes, including death, hydrocephalus, and long-term disability. 7. IVH originates in the germinal matrix, a highly vascularized region in the subependymal areas surrounding the lateral ventricles. The pathogenesis of IVH is multifactorial, involving fluctuations or acute increases in cerebral blood flow, poor vascular integrity, and extravascular factors. 8. Coagulation abnormalities have been implicated in the development of IVH in preterm infants. Very low birth weight (VLBW) infants often exhibit prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) compared to older infants. 9. Evidence suggests that preterm infants have immature hemostatic systems, with both quantitative and qualitative differences in coagulation factors such as fibrinogen compared to adults. Even term infants have coagulation profiles distinct from those of adults. 10. Coagulation factors are synthesized by the fetus starting at approximately 10 weeks of gestation and do not cross the placenta. Consequently, vitamin K-dependent factors, such as prothrombin, protein C, protein S, and factors VII, IX, and X, are present in very low concentrations in the fetus and do not reach adult levels until later in infancy or adolescence. 11. Vitamin K is tightly regulated during fetal life, with fetal levels being approximately one-tenth of maternal concentrations. This low level may reduce the risk of mutagenesis in rapidly proliferating cells. As a result, vitamin K is administered to all infants at birth to support coagulation. 12. Despite controversy regarding the role of coagulopathy in IVH development, some clinicians advocate treating preterm infants with coagulopathy or perceived coagulopathy to prevent or limit the progression of IVH. 13. Plasma transfusion is frequently administered prophylactically to preterm infants with abnormal coagulation studies or early signs of disease, with the belief that it may prevent bleeding or normalize coagulation. 14. Studies have shown that a significant proportion of plasma transfusions in preterm infants are given prophylactically without evidence of bleeding. For example, 63% of plasma transfusions in one study were administered prophylactically, and 58% of transfusions were based on abnormal coagulation studies without clinical bleeding. 15. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have reported mixed results regarding the efficacy of plasma transfusion in preventing IVH. While some studies have shown a reduction in IVH incidence, others have not demonstrated significant improvements in neurodevelopmental outcomes. 16. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) contains a variety of plasma proteins, including procoagulant and anticoagulant factors, acute phase proteins, immunoglobulins, complement, transport molecules, and albumin. However, the short half-life of certain factors, such as factor VII, limits their duration of action. 17. Plasma products can be derived from whole blood or plasmapheresis. The timing of freezing determines whether the product is classified as FFP or F24. Both products are stored at temperatures of -18°C or colder and are nearly equivalent, with slight differences in factor VIII and factor V levels. 18. Pathogen inactivation technologies, such as solvent-detergent treatment and methylene blue treatment, are used to enhance the safety of plasma products by reducing the risk of transfusion-transmitted infections. However, these methods may alter or reduce coagulation factor content. 19. Plasma transfusion is typically administered in doses of 10 mL/kg, although higher doses may be used. The volume of transfusion can impact hemodynamic status and fluid balance in preterm infants. 20. The potential benefits of plasma transfusion in preventing IVH may be related to its ability to stabilize hemodynamic circulation and prevent rapid fluctuations in blood pressure, which are associated with IVH. However, other fluids may achieve similar effects without the risks associated with transfusion. 21. Severe IVH is a major cause of long-term disability in preterm infants. Up to 50% of survivors with Grade III IVH and up to 75% of those with Grade IV IVH experience significant neurological sequelae. 22. This Cochrane Review aims to evaluate the efficacy of plasma transfusion in preventing IVH in very preterm neonates and to provide clinicians with robust evidence to guide clinical decision-making. Despite the perceived benefits of plasma transfusion, its actual efficacy in preventing IVH remains unclear. 23. The administration of plasma transfusion carries potential risks, including volume overload, infection, and transfusion reactions. A careful evaluation of the benefits and risks, as well as considerations of dosing, route, and duration of administration, is necessary. 24. Currently, no treatment exists for IVH once it has occurred. Most strategies focus on prevention or addressing underlying risk factors. Further research is needed to clarify the role of plasma transfusion in preventing IVH in high-risk preterm infants.
